title: The Ordinary Inventory
premise: Jonah Reyes, a bridge inspector whose meticulous measurements mask five years of unspoken grievances with his wife Elena, is summoned by Tomás Iriarte, the last fluent speaker of a dying Basque-adjacent language, to become his final student. As Jonah learns, he discovers the language holds an unwritten legal code — a system of justice that once governed a mining town where Tomás witnessed a killing that official courts never punished. Teaching the language means teaching the code, and the code demands restitution: the killer, now a respected developer, is about to demolish the last building where it all happened. Jonah must choose between preserving a language as artifact or activating it as instrument, and in doing so finally says what he has almost said to Elena for five years. The novel ends with the language's last sentence spoken aloud at the demolition site — not to save the building, but to name the crime before witnesses — leaving justice achieved outside law but inside memory, and Jonah's marriage measured honestly at last.
about_author: Mirabel Dunmore spent a decade working as a structural surveyor before turning to fiction, and her prose retains an engineer's patience for load-bearing detail. She lives near a river she has never trusted, writing about the quiet violence of things held too long.

chapters.title: Expansion Joints
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. We meet him measuring a deteriorating bridge while measuring, silently, the distance between himself and Elena over breakfast dishes and separate beds. A letter arrives from a man named Tomás Iriarte requesting 'one student, one season.' Emotional beat: the ache of precision without confession.

chapters.title: The Last Speaker
chapters.summary: Jonah visits Tomás in a cluttered house above the old mining valley. The old man tests him with riddles in a language Jonah has never heard yet half-understands. Tomás refuses to teach vocabulary first; he teaches grievance. POV: Jonah. Beat: fascination shadowed by unease.

chapters.title: Lessons in Grievance
chapters.summary: Alternating between lessons and Jonah's inspections, we learn the language has no word for 'forgive' but twelve for 'debt.' Elena notices Jonah coming home changed, humming syllables. POV: Jonah, with one Elena interlude. Beat: intimacy growing elsewhere while home thins.

chapters.title: What the Code Demands
chapters.summary: Tomás reveals the killing: 1968, a strike organizer beaten to death in the company hall; the foreman who did it was never charged. The language's justice code requires public naming before the place of the crime falls. POV: Jonah. Beat: horror braided with obligation.

chapters.title: The Developer
chapters.summary: Jonah researches the foreman's son — Aldous Merrick, now a developer whose firm owns the demolition permit for the old company hall. Jonah attends a planning meeting and sees how power launders history into 'revitalization.' POV: Jonah. Beat: cold recognition of respectable corruption.

chapters.title: Elena's Ledger
chapters.summary: Elena's POV chapter. She finds Jonah's notebook: grammar charts interleaved with unsent letters to her, five years of almost-sentences. She confronts him not with anger but with the notebook open on the table. Beat: devastating tenderness; the marriage's own debt named.

chapters.title: Demolition Date
chapters.summary: The permit is accelerated; the hall comes down in three weeks. Tomás's health fails faster. Jonah realizes he cannot learn enough in time — unless the final lesson is not fluency but witness. Tomás begins teaching him the single formal speech of accusation. POV: Jonah. Beat: rising panic under discipline.

chapters.title: The Broken Tongue
chapters.summary: Tomás suffers a stroke mid-lesson, losing the language even as he tries to give it away. In the hospital he can only mouth shapes. Jonah, half-fluent, must reconstruct the accusation speech from fragments, notes, and a 1968 recording. POV: Jonah. Beat: grief weaponized into resolve.

chapters.title: The Hall
chapters.summary: Climax. At the demolition site, before Merrick, workers, and a small crowd, Jonah speaks the accusation in a dying language he barely commands — imperfect, halting, but complete. He names the dead man, the act, the man who ordered it. Merrick's composure cracks on camera. Elena stands beside Jonah. Beat: terror transfigured into testimony.

chapters.title: One Final Student
chapters.summary: Resolution. The demolition proceeds anyway; the building falls, but the recording of the speech spreads, prompting a reopened inquiry and a memorial. Tomás dies having heard news of it. Jonah and Elena begin translating each other honestly. The last line: the language survives as one sentence, spoken twice, remembered. Beat: quiet, earned peace.
